author: Keystone Today
title: Christmas tree scouting report highlights disease and pest risks after wet weather in Pennsylvania
text:
The latest Christmas Tree Scouting Report released on May 27 describes recent cool, damp conditions across Pennsylvania that have created a favorable environment for fungal diseases in Christmas tree plantings. Multiple rainfall events and persistent humidity over the Memorial Day weekend led to prolonged leaf wetness, particularly affecting dense blocks of Fraser fir, spruce, and arborvitae.
Daytime temperatures ranged from the upper 50s to upper 60s with overnight lows dropping into the 40s and low 50s. These conditions were described as ideal for needlecast diseases and other fungal pathogens to infect new growth. The report states that while drier weather is forecasted for the next five days, growers should remain vigilant because infections from previous moisture may continue developing. The upcoming dry period is considered an opportunity for growers to complete fungicide applications and scout fields more thoroughly before another potential wet cycle.
Pest observations include active balsam twig aphids in untreated Fraser fir, settling elongate hemlock scale crawlers, presence of cryptomeria scale eggs but not yet crawlers in Cumberland County, ongoing spider mite activity especially as warmer weather approaches, and no new reports of bagworm activity this week. The report emphasizes timely treatment during pest vulnerability stages: “Treatment options are most effective while aphids remain active on tender expanding growth.” For cryptomeria scale management, it notes: “The most important factor with cryptomeria scale is timing applications to crawler emergence.”
Disease pressure remains high following recent wet periods with completed needlecast and spruce disease applications reported last week. Growers are advised to monitor susceptible species closely and maintain protective fungicide programs during extended wet periods. Regarding spotted lanternfly nymphs observed in southeastern counties this week, the report says, “At this stage, nymphs are highly mobile… While Christmas trees are not considered a primary host crop, growers should remain aware of SLF activity around field borders.”
Growers are reminded by the Pennsylvania Department of Agriculture that “the label is the law” regarding pesticide use compliance with federal and state regulations. Penn State Extension provides science-based education supporting agriculture—including workshops on farming practices and pest control—throughout all counties via local offices and digital tools; it collaborates with government agencies to deliver educational programming focused on agriculture, nutrition, environmental stewardship, and community well-being initiatives for individuals or businesses; these efforts foster innovation across Pennsylvania, according to Penn State Extension .
The next scouting report will be available June 3; observations can be submitted prior to noon on June 2.

The report states that while drier weather is forecasted for the next five days, growers should remain vigilant because infections from previous moisture may continue developing.
